subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday my leader (Mr. Bennett) in his brilliant and powerful speech expressed the views of the Conservative party on the principles and proposals involved in the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). Having regard to the policy of the government and the Liberal party during the past eleven years, knowing something of the free traders who are found in the ranks of the government supporters to-day, and realizing in many respects in the budget proposal the absence of sound economic principles for protecting the interests of Canada first, I say this budget is astounding; in fact it is more. It is a monster of political ingenuity, having the head of the American eagle carried low with a vacant look of expectant defeat in its eyes, with the mask of Cobden-the great free trader-on the right side of the head towards the Liberal-Progressives, and the mask of Sir John A. Macdonald and imperial trade on the left towards Ontario; its body is the Liberal party, bent and broken, and the only utterance of which this monster is capable, is, " Give me more votes, and I promise you everything." I think in a metaphorical way that sums up to some extent the involved and intricate measures in the budget proposals.
The Liberal party has suffered an astounding, yes, an amazing reversal of attitude so
The Budget-Mr. Ladner

far as their fiscal policies are concerned. The attitude of the public mind, well known to all those who study the political thought of Canada to-day, is one of approval of the policies which the Conservative party has advocated for a great number of years. In fact, it is more than that, it is an indication of the avalanche of public disapproval which is shortly to overwhelm the government.
My chief function to-day is to review the stand of the Liberal party with respect to its fiscal policy. As I have only forty minutes at my disposal, hon. members will pardon me if I hurry in reading these quotations because I desire to put them on record. In a pamphlet issued in October 1921, headed " Liberals and the Tariff," we find announced the fiscal policy of the Liberal party as far back as 1893. That is reiterated in a number of other pamphlets and official declarations of the Liberal party. In 1893, at the national Liberal convention which was held at Ottawa on June 20 and 21, two resolutions dealing with the tariff were unanimously adopted. Let me read the one dealing with tariff reform:
_ We, the Liberal party of Canada, in convention assembled declare:-
That the customs tariff of the Dominion should be based, not as it is now upon the protective principle, but upon the requirements of the public service.
That the existing tariff, founded upon an unsound principle, and used, as it has been by the government, as a corrupting agency, wherewith to keep themselves in office, has developed monopolies, trusts and combinations;
We do not hear so much about "monopolies, trusts and combinations" to-day since a certain hon. gentleman has gone to the Senate:
It has decreased the value of farm and other landed property;
It has oppressed the masses to the enrichment of a few;
It has checked immigration;
It has caused great loss of population;
It has impeded commerce;
It has discriminated against Great Britain. In _ these and in many other ways it has occasioned great public and private injury, all of which evils must continue to grow in intensity as long as the present tariff system remains in force.
That the highest interests of Canada demand a removal of this obstacle to our country's progress, by the adoption of a sound fiscal policy, which, while not doing injustice to any class, will promote domestic and foreign trade, and hasten the return of prosperity to our people;
That to that end, the tariff should be reduced to the needs of honest, economical and efficient government;
That it should be so adjusted as to make free, or to hear as lightly as possible upon the necessaries of life, and should be so arranged as to promote freer trade with the whole world, more particularly with Great Britain and the United States.

We believe that the results of the protective system have grievously disappointed thousands of persons who honestly supported it, and that the country, in the light of experience, is now prepared to declare for a sound fiscal policy.
The issue between the two political parties on this question is now clearly defined.
The government themselves admit the failure of their fiscal policy and now profess their willingness to make some changes, but they say that such changes must be based only on the principle of protection.
This is the concluding paragraph:
We denounce the principle of protection as radically unsound, and unjust to the masses of the people, and we declare our conviction that any tariff changes, based on that principle, must fail to afford any substantial relief from the burdens under which the country labours.
That was the primary declaration of policy on the fiscal question made by the Liberal party in 1893. The next important step, as revealed by this pamphlet, is what happened in 1896. It is as follows:
In 1896 when the Liberals came into office under Sir Wilfrid Laurier they at once appointed a tariff commission which fully investigated the exact economic situation in the country. They made a report the next year, 1897. Early in the session of that year the new Liberal government passed its first measure of tariff revision whereby 47 articles were added to the free list and duties reduced on 147 others, including farm implements.
At a convention of the Liberal party held in August of 1919 the following resolution was unanimously adopted:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance: first, diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second, reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all products of wheat; the principal articles of food; farm implements and machinery; farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils; nets, net twines and fishermen's equipments; cements and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries) as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.

The Budget-Mr. Ladner
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provision of thiR resolution when returned to power.
This is the result of avoiding extremes of view either one way or the other and as best suited to the whole of Canada with the country's various and varying interests.
In September, 1921, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a statement in respect to the tariff question in which he reiterated the same viewpoint. The remainder of my references will be taken from an even more authoritative source; I refer to Hansard of this chamber. It will be seen from that record that one of the first acts of the Prime Minister when he formed a government was to renounce his stand and the pledge of his party and to declare the fiscal policy to be merely a chart which he would follow if it were suitable. At page 2539 of Hansard of 1922, the present leader of the government when dealing with the tariff question during the debate on the budget referred to the Conservative tariff proposals of May, 1920. In his address he sets out the proposals and proceeds to condemn them. At page 2542 he makes certain specific statements which are rather interesting because it will be remembered that this was the first session in which the Liberal party had the opportunity to put their fiscal declaration into effect. The right hon. gentleman is quoted as follows:
But I might go a step further. Apart from that interpretation the Liberal party at the last session of parliament stated its position on the tariff very emphatically. . . I have in my hand the amendment moved. Here are the essential features of it, and I contend that every one of them has been carried out in the proposals of the Minister of Finance^-not in full, perhaps, but that every proposal is in accordance with what is here laid down.
Then the resolution to which he referred is set out, and I will ask Hansard to incorporate it in my remarks:
That while recognizing that existing financial requirements of the Dominion demand the maintenance of a customs tariff, the house is unable to concur in the declarations by the government that the tariff should be based on the principle of protection; the tariff is a tax, and the aim of legislation should be to make taxation as light as circumstances will permit;
That the aim of the fiscal policy of Canada should be the encouragement of industries based on the natural resources of the country, the development of which may reasonably be expected to create healthy enterprises giving promise of enduring success;
That such changes should be made in the customs duties as may be expected to reduce the cost of living, and to reduce also the cost of implements of production required for the efficient development of the natural resources of the Dominion;
That while keeping this aim clearly in mind the house recognises that in any readjustment
of the tariff that may take place regard must be had to existing conditions of trade, and changes made in such a manner as will cauoc the least possible disturbance of business.
Then the Prime Minister continues:
There is the position of the Liberal party as stated in the House of Commons, and that was the position which members of the party took throughout the campaign in setting forth their stand on fiscal reform and tariff revision.
Then again at page 2543 the right hon.
gentleman says:
The platform of 1919 was not put forward throughout this last campaign as a pledge or promise on the part of the Liberal party of its proposals if returned to power. . . it proves of itself than hon. gentlemen opposite know very well that throughout that campaign no effort was made to say that the Liberal platform as drafted in 1919 would constitute a promise and pledge to the electorate if the party were returned to power.
In that paragraph you will note a deliberate statement as to their platform of 1919 and a deliberate pledge that they would carry it out. One of the first utterances of the Prime Minister was to the effect that he would not carry it out. Then at page 2544 the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
It was further stated that the revision should be downwards, in the interests of producers and consumers, and that in such downward revision we would seek to lower the duties on the instruments of production in the basic industries and on the necessaries of life, with a view to increased production and a lessening of the cost of living to the masses of the people.
Then at the session of 1923 the Prime Minister in his address on the budget is reported as follows:
In the first place there are in it, so far as tariff matters are concerned, a very large number of reductions in duties. I have in my hand a list of tariff reductions in which some twenty-one different items have been affected by considerable reductions, apart altogether from the general reduction made through the British preference on all articles.
At page 3049 the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
Now, Mr. Speaker, when one considers that the essential features of this budget are: No increase in taxation; a substantial revision downwards of many items in the customs tariff; a large reduction so far as sugar is concerned; an increase in the British preference on all articles coming by way of Canadian ports; a revival of the offer of reciprocity to our neighbours to the south-when we consider these essential features how can it possibly be stated that this is a protectionist budget?
Then at page 3051 we find the following:
Does my hon. friend from Brome believe that Pitt, that Huskisson, that Peel, that Gladstone, that these great protagonists of free trade, never had ' their days of darkness, of
The Budget-Mr. Ladner

disappointment and of difficulty? Does he believe that these great statesmen never knew what it was to feel solitary and alone in their inability to realize within a limited period of time the ideal which was so strong in their own minds? Had these men seen well to divide themselves from their party, even to the limited extent to which my hon. friend has found it necessary so to do, would Gladstone's name, would Peel's name, would Huskisson's name stand out to day in history as they do as the men who brought about these great reforms in trade?
Hon. members will recall that at that time our good friend the Prime Minister was in serious difficulties so far as the support of this house was concerned, and he was endeavouring to elicit the support of his friends amongst the Progressive party. I presume the minister would seek to link his name with the names of the illustrious statesmen I have just mentioned.
During that speech on the budget in the session of 1924 the Prime Minister reiterated the same principle. I refer to page 2128:
I would ask the House to recall that it was a resolution moved and in fact drafted by the present Minister of Finance, and to note the emphasis it places upon, first: reduction in the tariff as the main object to be sought; second, its disavowal of protection as the principle upon which the tariff should be based; third, the aim of our fiscal policy as the encouragement of industries based on the natural resources of the country; and fourth, the reduction of such duties as may be expected to reduce the cost of living, and the cost of the implements of production.
Throughout this speech the Prime Minister seeks to reiterate his policy along those lines, and for five pages he quotes extracts from several Canadian newspapers, the effect of which is to show that the Liberal party stands for reduction in tariff and for the fulfilment of the previous declarations as embodied in the policy of 1919. The Edmonton Bulletin of November 16, 1921, reports a speech of the hon. gentleman at Regina, as follows:
His policy, he said, was one of downward revision with the lightening of the tariff burden on implements of production, on the basic industries and on necessities of life.
Again in 1925, as reported at page 2656 of Hansard, the leader of the government reasserted his opposition to the protective policy or anything in the way of increased duties, and reaffirmed the viewpoint which he had previously expressed.
In 1927 the Prime Minister did not speak on the budget, but in 1928 he spoke in the strongest possible terms, and never in any of his addresses in this house has he made a stronger advocacy of a downward revision than
LMr. Ladner.]
during his address of 1928. I refer hon. members to page 1282, where the Prime Minister said:
One reason why I am anxious to place on record what has been done in this regard is that the government with respect to the tariff has been following a consistent policy- of downward revision, and, in considering the budget presented this year, it is only right that it should be considered in relation to what has been done in previous years in the matter of tax reductions. I will give in a few moments what we did in respect to cottons and woollens a few years ago. This ought to be taken into account in connection with what is being done this year.
At the conclusion of that address there is set out a list of articles showing the reductions in duty from 1921 to 1928, including 196 specific articles in addition to many other articles of a like description on which the duty was reduced. Then at page 1289 the Prime Minister makes this extremely interesting and suggestive statement with respect to his fiscal policy:
May- I say just one further word in regard to the method by which the government has proceeded in the matter of tariff revision. I doubt if the government's method could be better described than as set forth in the resolution which was passed at the inter-parliamentary conference held in Paris on August 25, last year. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) referred to a resolution adopted by the League of Nations. That resolution laid stress on the importance of nations reducing rather than raising their customs tariff. We are proud of the fact that Canada stands out as the one country in the world that has pursued the course which was there advocated by all of them. In connection with the inter-parliamentary conference-which I understand is an inter-parliamentary conference of all the nations in the world-the following resolution was passed:
The twenty-fourth inter-parliamentary conference regrets to note a general tendency among the states to raise their customs tariffs. It recommends that the national groups shall endeavour to arrest and to reverse that tendency.
Another of the Paris recommendations completes this one by expressing the wish
"that methods of abolishing, or at least progressively and gradually reducing customs duties, be made an object of study in all countries..
The report goes on to say that such annual reduction could be sufficiently slight not to cause a crisis and to permit the different national industries to adopt themselves to the new conditions.
I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that it has been along these lines that the present administration has proceeded in reducing the customs tariff.
So, Mr. Speaker, in 1928 the Prime Minister and his party were consistently following the declarations made in 1893, 1919 and at every session of parliament from then until 1928.

The Budget-Mr. Ladner
Again in 1929 we had a reaffirmation of the government's stand on its fiscal policy. At page 1385 the Prime Minister says:
Strive as my hon. friend and his associates may not to credit the government with aught on account of this prosperity, they will have difficulty in having the country believe that the policies which we have put in force during the last seven years have not been in large part responsible for the progress which I have just mentioned.
So you will observe, Mr. Speaker, that as late as 1929 the Prime Minister and his government were still standing by what they considered to be a consistent policy, as enunciated in 1919. Then at page 1408 the Prime Minister said:

I hope hon. members will feel that neither amendment is at the present time in the national interest, but that it is very much m the interests of the country to allow the government to continue to carry out the policies which in the past have made for the increased prosperity which we enjoy to-day.
The Minister of Finance made a statement which is reported by Mr. A. G. Dexter in MacLean's Magazine of February 1, 1930. No doubt this is a considered statement of his own views. The article featured the extraordinary and commendable record of the personal success of the Minister of Finance since coming to this country. At the same time this article quotes the Minister of Finance as giving his statement of policy in these words:
We shall move forward cautiously toward the goal of making our tariff structure bear as lightly as possible on production, industry, and the people generally, having always in view the greater prosperity of all the legitimate industries of Canada.
The tariff must be made to serve the best interests of the Canadian people as a whole. It must be adjusted from time to time to meet the needs not of one class or group or industry alone, but of our whole economic structure. This does not mean tariff tinkering, so-called, but it does mean a continuous expert examination and adjustment whenever the facts so revealed warrant.
I commend these next words to the attention of hon. members:
The Liberal policy throughout the period of years since 1921 is the best evidence of what our policy is. We stand by our record in that regard. We intend to pursue that policy in future.
Such, Mr. Speaker, was the statement of the Minister of Finance of February 1 of this year, but since then what has happened? The government saw that it was inevitable that in the near future they should seek the approval of the people. It was apparent to them that the results of their economic policy had not worked to the advantage of the general masses of the people, but had been a contributing
factor in bringing about economic depression, a very large volume of unemployment, an adverse balance of trade of 8103,000,000 and a disturbance of our business activities which was calculated to put this country in a very serious condition. So, being faced with these facts, with characteristic political ingenuity and some knowledge of the approval by the people of politics which the Conservative party has supported for a long time, the Prime Minister and his government categorically, without explanation or excuse, reversed themselves, went back entirely upon their fiscal policy and brought into parliament a budget which involves proposals of great consequence to this country and which, as I said a moment ago, do not give consideration to the interests of Canada above those of all other countries.
It is not my intention to go into this phase of the matter, because it was dealt with very ably and completely by my leader yesterday. I make this statement, Mr. Speaker, that no policy is sound which does not work for the prosperity, for the comfort and for the happiness of the working people of this country. I would direct the attention of hon. members of this house to the official records of the government. There are two publications issued by the Department of Labour dealing with the prices of commodities in Canada and the wages and hours of labour. If hon. members will refer to the first document, they will find disclosed on pages 4 and 5 and at page 8 the fact that the cost of living in 1925 was higher than in any other year for the past eight years.
It will be noted that the purpose and idea of the fiscal policies of the Liberal party during the period from 1896 to 1919 was to lessen the cost of living. That was the aim of its fiscal policies, but the records of the government prove conclusively that it did not lessen the cost of living; it actually increased the cost of living to the people of this country.
Another consequence has been that while during the past eight years the cost of living has increased-the tariff question does not determine the cost of living, which seems to be an economic fallacy under which the members of the government labour-the wages paid in most of the industries of this country have not advanced. The document dealing with wages and hours of labour, referring to pages 39, 40, 41, 42, 43 and the following pages, and also to page 63, proves this to be the fast. It will be found in a great many instances that wages have been lowered to a considerable extent. That applies particularly to the common labourer who

He will find that rather difficult. I suggest that when the clang of battle sounds and our friends across the way take their positions in their constituencies, they maintain a single course in the matter of fiscal policy, in order that in a statesmanlike way we may find the reaction of the public mind on fiscal questions so that business may be stabilized, progress reestablished, the adverse balance of trade reversed; so that the great working masses of the country may find employment and Canada may go forward in a manner which in my judgment it will not do if the present government is returned to power.
On motion of Mr. Stevens the debate was adjourned.
